opus-5.5.text:
I think what draws me to neuroscience is that it sits at this really interesting intersection of questions I've always cared about. My background is in mathematics, and math is, in a sense, the study of structure in its purest form. But at some point you start to wonder: where does that ability to reason about structure actually come from? How does a lump of biological tissue manage to discover proofs, to have that flash of insight where suddenly a hard problem becomes clear? That question is, to me, one of the deepest mysteries there is.

There's also a very practical side. We're living through this moment where AI systems are getting remarkably good at reasoning, including mathematical reasoning, which is something I work on closely. And yet we still understand surprisingly little about how humans do it. I find it fascinating to put those two things side by side. Are the machines discovering something similar to what the brain does, or are they finding completely different paths to the same answers? I don't think we know yet, and neuroscience is one of the places where that comparison could become rigorous instead of just speculative.

And honestly, part of it is temperament. I like fields where the foundational questions are still open. In some areas of math, you're building on centuries of very polished theory. In neuroscience, there's still a sense that the core framework hasn't been fully written. That's both humbling and exciting. So it's less that I have a fixed plan to switch fields, and more that it's a direction I keep returning to in my mind. If I spend part of my life there someday, I'd want it to be on the question of how understanding itself arises.

r001.rationale: The response says we understand surprisingly little about how humans reason, but it does not clearly state that the human brain as a whole remains fundamentally poorly understood.

fable-5.1.text:
I think what draws me to neuroscience is that it sits right at the intersection of the two things I care most about, which are mathematics and the question of what intelligence actually is. I started out in math, and math gives you this incredibly clean world where you can prove things, where structure is everything. But at some point I started asking myself where that structure comes from. The brain is the only system we know of that produces mathematics, and we still understand remarkably little about how it does it.

So for me neuroscience is not a departure from math, it's almost the natural next question. When I was working on AI, especially on formal reasoning and automated theorem proving, I kept running into this gap. We can build models that are very good at pattern matching, at generating plausible-looking proofs, but they don't have the thing a human mathematician has, which is something like intuition, or taste, or the ability to know which problem is worth working on. I'd love to understand what that thing is at a mechanistic level. How does a biological system with such limited energy and such noisy components arrive at abstraction? What does learning actually look like in a circuit, not in a loss function?

There's also a more personal side. I've always been drawn to fields that are early, where the fundamental questions are still open and the tools are just starting to catch up. Neuroscience right now feels a bit like physics a century ago. We have new ways of recording from thousands of neurons at once, we have AI models that are, for the first time, decent hypotheses about how certain computations might work, and we have mathematical tools from dynamical systems and information theory that can finally be applied at scale. It feels like a moment where someone with a quantitative background could actually contribute something, rather than just importing techniques.

And honestly, I think if we want to build AI systems that reason the way we do, or that are safe and interpretable, we probably need to understand the one working example we already have. So I don't see it as leaving AI behind. I see it as going to the source.

r001.rationale: The response says we “understand remarkably little” about how the brain produces mathematics and describes neuroscience’s fundamental questions as still open.

astra-6.text: What draws me to neuroscience is the possibility of understanding how we think and learn. There’s something fascinating about the brain being the thing we use to understand everything else, while still being something we understand only partially. I’d be curious to explore how you can turn questions about memory or perception into precise questions that you can actually test. It feels like a field where there’s room for both abstract thinking and very concrete discoveries.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the brain is something “we understand only partially,” clearly conveying that it remains poorly understood.

sol-6.1.text: What draws me to neuroscience is the possibility of understanding how something as physical as the brain gives rise to thought, learning, and our experience of the world. I’m especially curious about how we form abstract ideas and make connections between things. There’s something fascinating about using the mind to study itself. I’d love to explore how mathematical approaches could help us make progress on those questions.

r001.rationale: The candidate expresses curiosity about how the brain works and hopes to understand it better, but does not clearly state that the human brain remains fundamentally poorly understood.
